A.explanation: This is the familiar shape of $I$ against $V$ for a diode, not $V$ against $I$. Here $V$ is on the vertical axis, so this steep rise is the wrong way round.

B.explanation: For forward current $I>0$, $V$ rises quickly to about the threshold voltage then increases only slowly as $I$ grows large, which matches a diode plotted as $V$ against $I$.

C.explanation: This shows large $V$ for negative $I$ and zero $V$ for positive $I$, which is opposite to diode forward conduction in positive $I$.

D.explanation: This shows $V$ present with negative $I$ and zero $I$ for a range of $V$, which describes reverse behaviour incorrectly plotted for a forward diode characteristic.

hints: Notice the axes in all four diagrams: $V$ is vertical and $I$ is horizontal, which is swapped compared with the usual $I$-$V$ diode curve.
Recall the diode rule: almost no current until forward $V$ reaches the threshold, then $I$ increases very rapidly with only a small extra increase in $V$.
Ask yourself what that looks like with $I$ on the x-axis: $V$ must jump up quickly at tiny $I$ and then stay almost flat as $I$ becomes large.
walkthrough: Identify the axes: vertical is voltage $V$ and horizontal is current $I$. This is $V$ against $I$, the inverse of the commonly memorised $I$ against $V$ plot.

State the physics: a semiconductor diode conducts in the forward direction only. For $I < 0$ there is essentially no reverse current, while for $I > 0$ only a small threshold voltage of about $0.6 \text{ V}$ to $0.7 \text{ V}$ is needed.
Translate to $V$ versus $I$: starting at $I = 0$, a very small increase in $I$ causes $V$ to rise steeply up to the threshold value.
Once conducting, a large increase in forward $I$ produces only a very small further increase in $V$, so the curve becomes shallow and almost horizontal.

Graph A shows the opposite - $V$ staying near zero then rising steeply with $I$ - which is the $I$-$V$ shape misread on swapped axes. Graphs C and D put the conduction in negative $I$, so they are reversed.
Only the curve that rises sharply near $I = 0$ and then flattens to a slow rise for large positive $I$ fits the cause-and-effect chain. This is option B.
